title: Last alfalfa irrigation before harvest; criteria for stopping and reducing water
excerpt: Practical criterion for stopping alfalfa irrigation before harvest: drainage of about 2 inches ET between the last irrigation and cutting in silt loam soil; growing-season consumption over 0.30 and fall consumption about 0.10 inches per day. Key point: alfalfa has no critical water-stress stage, but moisture between cuts must be controlled.
content_html:
Short answer: irrigation cutoff criteria

In practice, irrigation continues until there is sufficient time for the soil between cuts to dry out. In the climates studied, this time is about 2 inches of cumulative ET after the last irrigation; that is, continue irrigating until the soil between cuts drains sufficiently, then stop source.

Measured inputs

For decision-making, there are two reported numerical inputs:
• Growing-season consumption: more than 0.30 inches per day source
• Fall consumption: approximately 0.10 inches per day source
• Drainage required before cutting: 2 inches ET in silt loam soil of southern Idaho source

Note: These values are reported for climates of the western United States (Nebraska, southern Idaho, Utah). Conversion to centimeters is for display purposes only and is not by itself a basis for management recommendations.

Rationale for cutting and reducing water before harvest

Alfalfa, unlike many crops, does not have a specific critical growth stage for water stress. Under drought it enters dormancy and resumes growth after moisture returns source. For this reason, cutting irrigation before harvest generally does not harm the plant, but you should be careful:

  • the soil between cuts remains moist enough that fungi and crown rot do not become active
  • roots are nourished to store carbohydrates before winter cold

Field monitoring and timing criteria

The table below summarizes the decision criteria:

CriterionConditionRecommended action
ET drainage between irrigation and cuttingabout 2 inchesreportedSoil is ready for cutting
Growing-season consumption> 0.30 inches/dayContinue regular irrigation
Fall consumptionapproximately 0.10 inches/dayGradually reduce irrigation
Soil moisture monitoringSoil between cutsWait until sufficient drainage

Errors and scope of application

Common error:complete cessation of irrigation immediately before harvest without regard to soil moisture — this accelerates crown rot in the next cutting.
Regional scope:The above reports pertain to silt loam soils of the western United States. Always check soil texture, irrigation system, and local climate.
Timing uncertainty:The source does not provide an exact numerical range for "days to wait after last irrigation before cutting" across all soil textures source.

Fall water storage

In some climates, fall irrigation through November (before freeze-up) can provide deep water reserves for rapid spring growth next year source. This method aims to store deep water, not to maximize yield in the current season.

Reference

  • USU Extension – Strategies for Deficit Irrigation of Forage Crops
  • UNL CropWatch – Alfalfa Irrigation & Last Cutting
  • Alfalfa Symposium Proceedings – ET Before Cutting

faq.question: Can alfalfa regrow after irrigation is stopped before harvest?
faq.answer: Yes. Alfalfa, unlike many crops, has no specific critical growth stage for water stress; under drought it enters dormancy and resumes growth after moisture returns.

faq.question: How much ET drainage is needed before cutting?
faq.answer: In silt loam soils of southern Idaho, about 2 inches of cumulative ET after irrigation and before cutting has been reported as sufficient for adequate soil drying.

faq.question: What is the purpose of fall irrigation?
faq.answer: Fall irrigation through November (before freeze-up) can provide deep water reserves for rapid spring growth next year; the goal is water storage, not maximizing yield in the current season.
